questions.q: How does SMOTE create a new minority-class row?
options: It copies an existing minority row exactly
It picks a minority row and one of its nearest minority neighbors, and adds a point on the line between them
It deletes a random majority row
It averages every minority row into one
questions.explain: SMOTE interpolates between a minority point and one of its k nearest minority neighbors (k_neighbors=5 by default), producing new synthetic rows instead of exact copies.

questions.q: Why is 'SMOTE the whole training set, then cross-validate' wrong?
options: SMOTE cannot run on training data
Cross-validation only works on balanced data
Validation folds then contain synthetic near-copies of training rows and are artificially balanced, inflating the scores
It makes the model train more slowly
questions.explain: Synthetic points are derived from real ones, so information leaks between training and validation parts. In the lesson, recall looked like 0.983 instead of the honest 0.888.

questions.q: Which tool lets you place a resampler as a step ahead of a model inside cross-validation?
options: sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline
imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline
pandas.concat
sklearn.dummy.DummyClassifier
questions.explain: scikit-learn's Pipeline does not allow steps that change the number of rows. imblearn's Pipeline accepts samplers and applies them only during fit.

questions.q: Should you resample the test set before scoring the final model?
options: Yes, so the classes are balanced
Yes, but only with undersampling
Only if recall is below 0.5
No, the test set should stay untouched and reflect real data
questions.explain: The test set must look like production data, which is imbalanced. The imblearn pipeline skips resampling at predict time, and you should never resample held-out data.

questions.q: In the lesson, undersampling raised test recall to 0.848 but dropped precision to 0.683. What is the best reading?
options: Undersampling is always best
The model became a better ranker overall
Resampling moved the operating point along the precision-recall trade-off; choose it only if a miss costs more than false alarms
Precision does not matter on imbalanced data
questions.explain: Average precision was almost unchanged, so the ranking quality did not improve. Resampling traded precision for recall, which is worthwhile only when misses are the costlier error.
